title: Why your agents need decision traces, not just documents — Zach Blumenfeld, Neo4j

primary.label: Retrieval, Search & Knowledge
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 59%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on context graphs as an extension of RAG, featuring graph embeddings, hybrid search, and Neo4j-based knowledge-base design for agent retrieval. The tool is cross-domain with 22 built-in domains, directly serves knowledge-base and retrieval use cases, and provides a developer scaffolding platform. The project is newly launched with features like automated decision trace writing still in development. The talk assumes familiarity with graph databases, RAG, and embeddings but explains concepts through accessible demos. Conference presentation with live demonstrations, recorded demo playback, and Q&A. All supporting evidence is directly stated in the transcript with verified character offsets.

summary: Zach Blumenfeld, recently moved into a research engineering role at Neo4j after technical marketing, presents context graphs as an advancement over conventional knowledge bases used in RAG. While a knowledge base helps an agent answer questions correctly, a context graph provides the information needed to make better decisions—past decision traces, precedents, causal chains, and reasoning behind outcomes. He illustrates with a financial analyst agent that, rather than merely assigning a risk score, can recommend accept or reject by retrieving past decisions and their structural relationships from the graph. Context graphs contain entities (things that exist), events (decisions, transactions, approvals), and context (policies and reasoning recorded by both AI and humans). A key innovation is graph embeddings: connected decision trace nodes are embedded into vectors so structurally similar past decisions can be retrieved via vector similarity, supplementing traditional text-based semantic search. The demo uses Claude in the agent runtime, OpenAI embeddings, and Neo4j with GDS for graph embeddings, with a Next.js frontend. Zach then introduces `uvx create-context-graph`, a one-command scaffold that generates a full-stack application with backend, frontend, demo data, and an MCP server. It ships with 22 built-in domains (healthcare, FinServ, etc.) or can generate a custom ontology from a described domain. Supported frameworks include Pydantic AI, OpenAI, LangGraph, Crew, Strands, Google ADK, and Microsoft Agent Framework. Data connectors allow importing from GitHub, Notion, Jira, and Slack. The underlying Neo4j agent memory package provides three layers: short-term conversation history, long-term extracted entities that are deduplicated and resolved over time, and reasoning traces. Entity extraction follows a spaCy-to-GLiNER-to-LLM pipeline with separate merging, deduplication, and enrichment stages. Predefined domains use POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) entity and relationship types to guide extraction and mapping. Timestamps can be added to decision traces, with events linked by causal or temporal relationships (caused, next). Structured data such as CSVs or tables can be mapped directly via Cypher statements, while unstructured data flows through the entity extraction pipeline. The project is open source and newly launched; writing new decision traces automatically is still in development, currently requiring explicit prompting. A hosted live application is available for exploration, though conference Wi-Fi blocked access.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and context graph definition
sections.summary: Zach introduces himself and Neo4j, polls the audience on context graph familiarity, and defines context graphs as an evolution of knowledge bases that include information needed to make better decisions, not just answer questions.

sections.title: Financial analyst agent example
sections.summary: Uses a financial analyst agent to contrast a standard knowledge base response (risk score, review, risk factors) with a context graph response (accept/reject with reasoning). Context graphs contain entities, events, and context including policies and human/AI reasoning.

sections.title: Demo recording and hybrid search
sections.summary: Shows a recorded demo of the financial agent querying Jessica's profile, pulling decision traces, and running find precedents via hybrid search combining semantic and structural similarity in the graph.

sections.title: Graph embeddings explanation
sections.summary: Explains graph embeddings as embedding connected green nodes into vectors so similar decision traces can be retrieved by vector similarity, surfacing patterns hard to extract from documents alone.

sections.title: create-context-graph scaffolding tool
sections.summary: Introduces uvx create-context-graph as a one-command boilerplate generator with backend, frontend, demo data, and MCP server. Supports 22 domains and multiple frameworks. Live demonstration with healthcare domain and Pydantic AI.

sections.title: Neo4j agent memory package
sections.summary: Describes the underlying Neo4j agent memory package with three layers—short-term conversation history, long-term extracted entities, and reasoning traces—and the spaCy-to-GLiNER-to-LLM entity extraction pipeline with deduplication and merging.

sections.title: Q&A and additional details
sections.summary: Covers links to hosted live application and GitHub repo. Notes Microsoft Agent Framework integration alongside Google ADK. Q&A addresses timestamps on decision traces with causal/temporal links (caused, next), POLE entity types used in predefined domains, ontology preparation from descriptions for custom domains, structured vs unstructured data handling (Cypher mapping vs entity extraction), and ongoing development of automated decision trace writing which currently requires explicit prompting.
